newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Fuel surcharges dominate Dutch air freight market.
newsitem.headline: Fuel surcharges dominate Dutch air freight market.

text.p: Rates are strong in an active seasonal Amsterdam air cargo market but background talk still easily swings back to the still controversial way in which fuel surcharges were imposed, a Reuters survey showed.

Schiphol's cargo community is rushed off its feet enjoying the peak season and apart from ill feeling about surcharges, the Amsterdam market is undoubtedly booming, shippers, carriers and forwarders said.
Many shippers and forwarders claim it is no coincidence that the surcharges were introduced during the peak season.
Currently, few people want to talk about market activity as they are too busy filling aircraft and once they do have time it is impossible to talk about anything else other than surcharges.
All markets have seen rates increase, even without the surcharges and most carriers are full to overflowing so that the cost of air freighting is the highest for industry sources said.
A few carriers have implemented rates rises rather than surcharges. Martinair introduced increases of five to ten percent and Cathay Pacific increased its rates by ten guilder cents per kilo.

Tijn Middendorp trade director of leading forwarder, MSAS, said the market is "crazy" to the Middle East, Asia and the U.S. He added that sometimes space has to be asked for two weeks in advance and there has been some back-log of shipments.
The U.S. is especially busy with mail for Christmas and the beaujolais season firmly in place, said one forwarder.
Cathay Pacific's cargo manager, Achim van der Graaff, said the market to Hong Kong is very healthy and October this year was better than 1995 and November was showing strong signs of growth.

Perhaps, the only market where there was some possible doubt about the strength of rates was South Africa because several carriers have entered the market for the first time, such as Martinair and Virgin.
But Martinair's cargo rates increase seems to have assured a steady rate. South African Airways cargo manager Frits de Bois said that the market had high load factors and that rates are stable.
But despite the booming market the surcharge issue continues to dominate conversation.

In Amsterdam, any hopes by the forwarders and shippers that some carriers would not chose to implement surcharges have been pretty much dashed, as another batch of carriers announce that they too are introducing surcharges.

Varig Brazilian Airlines, South African Airways and Garuda Indonesia, had held out and they were making themselves the forwarders favourites, but all three will now be inposing surcharges on December 1. Royal Jordanian is one of the few carriers left not to have introduced a surcharge.

Forwarders and shippers had started divereting freight to intergrators who had not imposed surcharges but last week Federal Express announced an ex-Europe surcharge from December 1. But United Parcels Service and DHL Worldwide Express said they would not. Another major intergrator TNT Express Worldwide said it may have to consider some form of surcharge.
Surcharges have, ironically, made all sectors of the industry much more willing wants to talk about levels rates were at thus increasing market transparency.

The big difference in attitude concerns the timing of the charges. Forwarders and shippers understand carriers have got to recuperate costs incurred because of rising fuel costs but object to the short notice given whilst some share a belief that airlines action was co-ordinated once KLM introduced its surcharge.

Hans Knuvers, spokesman for the Dutch freight forwarders association, ATAN said: "Everybody is complaining but at the same time the forwarders recognise that the fuel prices have increased," adding that Dutch forwarders and shippers are united in their concerns over the "over night" imposition of surcharges.
Gino Laan, an Amsterdam marketing executive at Japan's all-cargo Nippon Cargo Airline said "in Japanese yen terms we have seen a 32 percent increase in fuel costs over the past few months."
"In the past the industry was regulated by competition rules from Brussels and IATA. But now there are no real guidelines, so this has resulted in the current situation, Knuvers said."
"Surcharges are never a nice thing but we are definitely looking for better guidelines in the future so this can be avoided and we are in regular contact with the shippers," he added.

Essentially the carriers have done themselves a great deal of damage as for an industry that claims that it wants to build up long-term trusting relationships with each other, this is no way to behave, said another forwarder.

Jos Busscher, director of ChartAir, one of Schiphol's leading forwarders, said: "These surcharges have been handled in an extremely amateurish way. Air freight bills for shippers have gone up overnight and we have to defend this position to our clients."

"Companies like IMB, Philips, Compaq give the airlines millions of guilders of business a year. This has not been handled in a professional way. If a reasonable time of notice was given shippers could pay in instalments." he added.
"Hopefully this will lead to more transparency over rates. More understanding is needed, not these shocks or overnight surprises."

Kees van der Vleuten, air transport manager of Philips, said there had been no negotiation with the manufacturer or explanation concerning the level of surcharges and the absence of notice hit Philips as it had just finished their bi-annual rates negotiations with the carriers. Then two weeks later the surcharges started to be introduced, he added.
"We have had no time to prepare ourselves. We can't charge this on to our customers."
The industry needs a professional rates adjustment structure to cope with these increases, he stressed.

Van der Vleuten said shippers need explanations and a chance to negotiate. At the moment carriers are in a strong position but shippers and forwardsers said this that in the new year after the seasonal rush the situation may be very different. -- Air Cargo Newsroom Tel+44 171 542 7706 Fax+44 171 542 5017
